title: SAFE Kids vs. SMART Kids: Is the Philippines ready?
summary: MANILA, Philippines – I attended “SAFE Kids, SMART Policies: A Dialogue on Children’s Online Safety and Digital Rights,” organized by Gorriceta Africa Cauton & Saavedra at The Manila House on…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – I attended “SAFE Kids, SMART Policies: A Dialogue on Children’s Online Safety and Digital Rights,” organized by Gorriceta Africa Cauton & Saavedra at The Manila House on Thursday, October 22, to help get the discussion going and give the media, industry leaders, and fellow parents a better understanding of the two bills: the SAFE Kids Act and the SMART Kids Act.
The discussion raised an important question for me: beyond deciding which bill offers better protection for children, are we building a comprehensive system that can actually keep them safe online?

The conversation around children’s online safety often comes down to a comparison between restrictions and digital freedom. Which policy offers better protection? Which approach gives children more room to explore the internet while keeping them safe from its dangers?

But after considering the discussion surrounding the SAFE Kids Act and the SMART Kids Act, I find myself asking a bigger question: Are we building a comprehensive system to protect Filipino children, or are we once again trying to solve a complex problem with a partial solution?
It is easy to compare two bills and determine which one appears better on paper. It is much harder to ask whether the country is prepared to implement either of them effectively.
Beyond restrictions: Where do parents fit into the equation?

One of the most important aspects of children’s online safety is the role of parents. Yet, when we discuss legislation, the conversation often revolves around restrictions, penalties, platform accountability, and the responsibility of technology companies.
These are all important considerations. However, where in the legislation do we address the need to educate parents themselves?

Will digital parenting become part of the seminars that couples attend as they prepare for parenthood? Will it be incorporated into existing parenting programs under local government units or relevant government agencies? Will parents receive practical guidance on recognizing online exploitation, discussing sensitive digital experiences with their children, identifying misinformation, and setting healthy boundaries around technology?
And if these programs already exist, how accessible are they, and how effective have they been?

We cannot assume that every parent understands the digital environment their children are navigating. Some grew up alongside technology, while others are still learning how social media, online gaming, artificial intelligence, and digital communities work. Telling parents to protect their children without equipping them with the knowledge to do so risks making parental responsibility another obligation without adequate support.

At the end of the day, it is not just about the technology a child uses or the environment they grow up in. It is also about how informed and equipped their parents are to help them process the information they encounter.

A parent can be present, absent, supportive, neglectful, informed, or uninformed. These differences can shape how children understand and respond to the world around them. This is not about placing the entire burden of online safety on children or their parents. Rather, it is about recognizing that legislation alone cannot replace the guidance children need at home.

We also have to ask ourselves: What values are we demonstrating to our children? How do we teach accountability, critical thinking, empathy, and responsible technology use when we are still learning how to practice these things ourselves?
Protecting children must also mean educating the adults responsible for protecting them.
Digital rights must account for economic realities
Another concern is whether digital restrictions consider the realities of Filipino families.
When looking at other countries’ policies, we should consider not only online safety and education but also working-age laws, economic conditions, and the support available to families.
For some minors, the internet is more than entertainment. It can be a way to earn money, develop skills, create content, and support their families.

Consider the SMART Kids Act’s proposed blanket ban on social media access for those under 18. While protecting children from exploitation is important, treating all minors the same overlooks their different ages and circumstances.

A 16- or 17-year-old earning through legitimate content creation or creative work has different needs from a much younger child who may be more vulnerable to exploitation. If we take away these opportunities without providing alternatives, could some young people turn to less regulated or more dangerous ways to earn money?

The SAFE Kids Act’s tiered approach considers different factors, offering a way to balance children’s safety with their varying needs and circumstances. With proper safeguards, it could help distinguish harmful online activities from legitimate, age-appropriate opportunities.

Ultimately, protecting children should not mean ignoring the economic realities they face. If our goal is to prevent exploitation, we must do more than restrict access. We must also address the circumstances that make children vulnerable in the first place.
Accountability should not stop with platforms and parents

Discussions about children’s online safety understandably emphasize technology companies’ accountability. Platforms must be expected to implement appropriate safeguards, protect users’ information, respond to abuse, and take meaningful steps to prevent foreseeable harm.
Parents must also be supported in fulfilling their responsibilities. But what about the children themselves?

Accountability is an important part of growing up. Children need to understand that their actions online have consequences, whether they involve cyberbullying, harassment, spreading harmful content, violating another person’s privacy, or participating in other forms of online misconduct.

Of course, accountability must match a child’s age, maturity, circumstances, and capacity to understand the consequences of their actions. It should not mean treating children like adults or imposing punitive measures without considering their development.
Instead, the goal should be to help children understand responsibility, repair harm where possible, and learn from their mistakes.
This raises another question: If we are strengthening the rules that govern children’s digital behavior, are we also prepared to strengthen the systems that teach and enforce accountability?

The Philippines already has a juvenile justice framework under Republic Act No. 9344, as amended by Republic Act No. 10630. However, the existence of a law does not automatically mean that its implementation is adequate, accessible, or consistently effective.

Before adding another layer of restrictions, we should examine whether existing juvenile justice, intervention, rehabilitation, and educational systems are sufficiently equipped to address the realities of digital misconduct.

How do we ensure that a child who causes harm online receives appropriate consequences while also having an opportunity to learn and rehabilitate? How do we protect victims without overlooking the developmental needs of children who commit offenses?

These questions deserve attention alongside the discussion of digital restrictions. Otherwise, we risk creating rules without adequately preparing the institutions responsible for putting them into practice.
Why are we moving forward when the broader legal framework still has gaps?
We must also look beyond legislation specifically designed for children and acknowledge the gaps in our existing online safety laws.

Filipinos continue to face online scams, identity theft, harassment, fraud, and privacy violations. While the Philippines has laws covering cybercrime, data privacy, and online transactions, having these laws in place does not automatically mean that victims are adequately protected.

Challenges remain in public awareness, reporting mechanisms, law enforcement, and the investigation of increasingly complex online offenses. Many Filipinos may not know where to report incidents or what steps to take when they become victims. Meanwhile, technology continues to evolve, creating new risks that existing laws and enforcement systems may struggle to address.

These gaps raise a bigger concern: are we doing enough to strengthen our existing legal framework and the institutions responsible for enforcing it? Passing legislation is only the first step. Effective implementation requires funding, coordination among government agencies, public education, and consistent enforcement.

If we want to make the digital world safer for children, we must also address the weaknesses in the systems meant to protect everyone online. Child protection cannot exist in isolation from the country’s broader cybersecurity and online safety efforts.
The bigger question: Are we building a system or applying a band-aid?
Comparing the SAFE Kids Act and the SMART Kids Act is only the beginning. The bigger question is whether our country is ready to implement these policies effectively.

Passing a law is one thing. Educating parents, involving schools and local governments, funding enforcement, and ensuring that children’s digital rights are protected are different challenges altogether.

We also need to consider whether our existing cybersecurity and online safety systems are equipped to support these new policies. If gaps in enforcement, public awareness, and existing laws remain unresolved, introducing another law may not be enough.

Protecting children requires more than restrictions. It requires digital literacy, educated parents, accountable platforms, accessible reporting systems, and support for families. We must also ensure that children understand their responsibilities online and that policies do not unintentionally harm those who rely on legitimate digital opportunities.

Yes, the point is to make our kids safer. But are we prepared to make these policies work, or are we simply applying another band-aid solution to the country’s existing online safety and cybersecurity problems?

Comparing the two bills is one thing. Building a system that can effectively protect Filipino children is another. Our responsibility does not end with passing a law. It begins with making sure that the law actually works.
As a future parent, I cannot rely on legislation alone
Perhaps the most personal part of this conversation is realizing that, as a future parent, I will still have to prepare my child for an imperfect digital world.
I will have to teach them how to recognize harmful information, question what they see online, protect their privacy, respect other people, and ask for help when something does not feel right.
I will have to explain that not everything they encounter online is true, that not everyone they meet has good intentions, and that technology can be useful without always being safe.

I will also have to make sure they understand that restrictions are not substitutes for judgment. Eventually, children grow older, gain independence, and make decisions without their parents watching over them. The goal cannot simply be to keep them away from every possible danger. It must also be to prepare them to recognize and respond to danger when it appears.
And I know that the responsibility will not fall on me alone. Schools, communities, technology companies, and the government all have a role to play.

But the reality is that these institutions will have limitations. Laws may have loopholes. Platforms may fail to detect harmful content. Reporting systems may not always work as expected. Technology will continue to evolve faster than regulations can reasonably keep up.
As a parent, I cannot assume that every gap will be addressed before my child encounters it.

That is why parental education, digital literacy, and a culture of accountability matter just as much as the restrictions themselves. We need to raise children who can navigate the digital world, not simply children who have been temporarily shielded from it.
